explainer_content.short_definition: A stripped 1950s guitar-and-slapback lane where country boogie, blues, R&B, and hillbilly flash become urgent rock records.
explainer_content.history_capsule: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish. Sun Records is the best-known center, but the vocabulary spreads through Carl Perkins, Gene Vincent, Johnny Burnette, Eddie Cochran, Duane Eddy, Link Wray, and other records that make guitar attitude the event.
explainer_content.why_it_mattered: It preserved the rough edge inside early rock and roll. Later garage, punk, roots rock, psychobilly, and guitar revival styles all return to its compression, echo, and combustible swagger.
explainer_content.what_made_it_distinct: Compared with broader early rock, this lane feels more wiry and local: slapped bass, echo, hiccuped vocals, lean drums, sharp guitar breaks, and very little orchestral cushion.
what_to_listen_for: A walking or slapped upright bass
Short guitar figures that act like hooks
Country bends rubbing against blues rhythm
Records that sound spontaneous rather than arranged
